quests.hint: It's related to 'passage' — remember the double 's': PAS-SEN-GER.
quests.explanation: Related to 'passage' (a journey), 'passenger' keeps the double 's' from the same Latin root 'passare,' meaning 'to pass.'
Border control 'customs' comes from the same root as 'custom' (a habitual practice), with a silent 't' before the final 's.'
The prefix 'con-' often doubles its final letter when joined to a root starting with the same sound, as seen here in 'connection.'
This travel term describes a stop where you 'lay over' (rest) between flights, combining two simple words.
Related to Latin 'turba' (crowd or disturbance), 'turbulence' describes rough, disturbed air during a flight.
Dropping the final 'e' before adding '-ion' is a standard pattern, as in 'navigate' to 'navigation.'
This compound word describes a specific 'point' where your documents or bags are 'checked' before continuing.
The prefix 'mal-' means 'bad' or 'wrong,' so a malfunction is literally something functioning 'badly.'
Unlike 'software' which can change easily, 'firmware' is more permanently ('firmly') fixed into a device's hardware.
When an adjective ends in '-ible,' the noun form usually changes to '-ibility,' as in 'compatible' to 'compatibility.'

quests.hint: Remember the single 's' before final 'is': DIAG-NO-SIS.
quests.explanation: From Greek 'dia-' (apart) and 'gignoskein' (to know), a diagnosis is literally 'knowing apart' or distinguishing one illness from another.
Related to 'flame,' inflammation describes tissue that's 'inflamed' or heated, and the double 'm' comes from the Latin root 'flammare.'
The prefix 'im-' here intensifies the root 'mune' (service or duty) — being immune means being exempt from a duty or attack.
The root 'fract' means 'broken' (as in 'fraction'), so a fracture is literally a 'broken' bone.
'Cardio' relates to the heart, and 'vascular' relates to blood vessels — together describing the entire heart-and-vessel system.
Dropping the final 'e' before adding '-ion' is the same pattern as 'navigate' to 'navigation.'
Related to 'respire' (to breathe), this adjective describes anything connected to the breathing system.
The suffix '-ist' describes a person devoted to a particular field, as in 'special' becoming 'specialist.'
The suffix '-ation' turns the verb 'present' into a noun describing the formal act of presenting information.
The prefix 'multi-' means 'many,' so multitasking literally means handling 'many tasks' at once.
The suffix '-ity' turns the adjective 'punctual' into an abstract noun describing that quality of being on time.
This simple, transparent compound word joins 'work' and 'place' with no spelling changes.
The suffix '-ship' (as in 'relationship') describes a position or status, here describing the temporary training role of an intern.
Simply add '-ing' to the noun-turned-verb 'network,' describing the act of building professional connections.
The most commonly forgotten letter here is the second 'r' — 'curriculum' has a double 'r' in the middle, unlike many similar-sounding words.
Related to 'orient' (to find your bearings), an orientation session helps you get 'oriented' in a new job or place.
The suffix '-ary' turns the noun 'probation' into an adjective describing a trial period before something becomes permanent.
Just like 'apply' to 'application,' verbs ending in '-y' change to '-i' before adding '-cation.'
The suffix '-ment' turns the verb 'assess' (to evaluate) into a noun describing the evaluation process itself.
Like 'internship,' this word uses '-ship' to describe a structured training position, here specifically for learning a trade.
